neighbours.label: the verb (come/go/enter) at the point where a law or agreement is about to 'come into force/effect'
fire: The revised building code will come into force on 1 March.
Under its final article, the convention enters into force ninety days after signature.
The trade pact between the two countries came into effect last summer.
Once the amendment goes into effect, landlords must register every tenancy.
New emission limits for trucks come into force across the bloc in July.
The armistice went into effect at eleven o'clock that morning.
The charter entered into force after two thirds of the members approved it.
Stricter visa rules came into force at the start of the year.
quiet: The revised building code was debated for three hours by the council.
Under its final article, the convention is open for signature by any state.
The trade ministers of the two countries came into the room smiling.
Once the amendment was drafted, landlords complained to the newspapers.
New trucks with cleaner engines come into the depot every July.
The armistice was celebrated with bonfires that morning.
The delegates entered into a long argument about the wording of the charter.
Stricter visa rules were criticised by the tourism industry.

notes: Card: peaks on ' come', ' went', ' enter(ed)', ' came' before 'into force/effect' for treaties and rules; the - pole promotes ' come', ' entered', ' into'. Probes: 'come into force' 0.79, 'entered into force' 0.81, 'went into effect' 0.26; 'came into the kitchen' 0.00, 'take effect' 0.11. 'The law will be enforced' gave 0.48 on ' will', so the pole anticipates the idiom; near misses use the same verbs with other subjects, or the same laws with another predicate.
